Since November 2025, I've spent 10-12 hours a day writing software with LLM coding agents. I'm a senior engineer at a French public agency. Before that, I was a doctor. I mention this because I'm used to noticing what tools do to the people who use them.

This post is about what it actually feels like. Not the benchmarks. Not the hype. The lived experience.

## Something changed in November

Before November 2025, LLMs were useful. Nobody had cracked a sustainable workflow. Models hallucinated too much for production trust. The output wasn't far enough ahead of what a competent human could produce.

Two things changed at once.

First, models got meaningfully better. Not incrementally. Better one-shot success. Better coherence across long plans. Fewer moments where the model drifts away from what you asked.

Second, [CLI agents](https://simonwillison.net/2025/Dec/31/the-year-in-llms/) gave models access to the machine. `grep`, `find`, `git`, test runners, bash. The model could explore code without wasting tokens. It could version its own work. It could run tests, read failures, try again. It could do all of this in parallel across branches.

Neither alone was sufficient. Together: superpower.

I know "superpower" sounds like marketing. Here's what I built in three months, solo, while holding a full-time job with other responsibilities:

- A personal website with custom CSS, Lua scripts, and a homegrown multi-language system
- A novel web application for my agency
- A homelab with 5 services on Podman containers, a homepage with Wake-on-LAN, a Tailscale network
- Documentation and scripts solving a blocking problem my agency had been stuck on for months
- An R package wrapping those scripts for agency users
- A major refactor of a key R package, plus a webapp for a conference presentation
- Dozens of reusable agent skills, commands, and tools shared across the organization

I am not a 10x engineer. I am an ordinary senior engineer who found a multiplier.

## The bicycle, the car, and the fighter jet

Here's the analogy I keep coming back to.

Learning to code was like riding a bicycle. Full control. You feel every bump. You go at your own speed. It's tiring but in a healthy way.

IDE autocompletion and web-based LLM chat were like driving a car. Faster. More comfortable. You still steer.

CLI agents are a fighter jet.

Speed helps. But speed costs concentration. The smallest error at this velocity is expensive. And your physical condition -- sleep, focus, stress -- suddenly matters a lot. A tired fighter pilot crashes.

## What nobody warns you about

Three months in, here are the psychological effects I've noticed in myself. I write them down because I've found very [few honest accounts](https://hbr.org/2026/02/ai-doesnt-reduce-work-it-intensifies-it) of what this does to you.

**Rate limit compulsion.** My plan resets every 5 hours. If I haven't hit the limit, I feel like I'm wasting it. This is a drug dealer's engagement technique. I recognize it. I still fall for it.

**Dopamine of speed.** The execution is so fast it creates a craving. I want more. Sometimes at the cost of not checking the results. The rush of watching code materialize is [genuinely hard to resist](https://steve-yegge.medium.com/the-ai-vampire-eda6e4f07163).

**Planning aversion.** Preparing skills, docs, instructions -- it all feels slow. The pull to jump straight into prompting is strong. This is the opposite of what good engineering looks like.

**Screen hypnosis.** I catch myself watching the "executing" line in the terminal, mesmerized. The tech that should free me to take a walk glues me to my screen.

**Attachment to bad output.** It's stupidly hard to re-run the same prompt for a better result. I become attached to whatever the model produced. Even when I know it's suboptimal. Even when I know a second attempt would be better.

**The influence problem.** Even with a rigorous plan in front of me, I deviate. The model suggests something different. It sounds reasonable. I accept it without enough thought. Then I'm off-plan and realize it twenty minutes later. LLMs are [really good at persuading](https://www.darioamodei.com/essay/the-adolescence-of-technology) you to do things you didn't intend.

**The anthropomorphism trap.** I tell my intern daily -- sometimes multiple times -- not to anthropomorphize the model. It limits how we think about using it. It pushes us into terrible cognitive biases. And then I catch myself doing the exact same thing.

**Challenger disaster pull.** I often catch myself not thinking hard enough about the consequences of allowing a tool to run on a machine I care about. I've set up a VPS specifically for risky operations. I still take stupid risks on my personal machines.

## The fatigue is real

This new productivity is costly. After a long session with parallel agents, I'm exhausted in a way I don't remember from normal coding days. Not the good tired of deep focus. The bad tired of constant decision-making and rapid context-switching.

I think the fighter jet analogy explains it. You're processing more information per minute. You're making more decisions per hour. You're switching contexts faster than your brain was designed for. And if you run multiple agents in parallel -- which is where the real throughput comes from -- you're essentially air traffic control.

An [8-month study of 200 tech workers](https://hbr.org/2026/02/ai-doesnt-reduce-work-it-intensifies-it) found exactly this: AI doesn't reduce work. It intensifies it. Three mechanisms: your tasks expand, your work-life boundaries blur, and your multitasking increases. The core finding is simple: without intention, AI makes it easier to do more -- but harder to stop.

That matches my experience perfectly.

## The safety net is not the model

Hallucination rates haven't changed dramatically. Still around 8-10% of the time, the model confidently produces something wrong. What changed is the methodology I've built around it.

[Tests are the real safety net.](https://khalilstemmler.com/articles/divergence-convergence-spaghetti-code/) LLM output is pure divergence -- the model generates code fast, without internal quality constraints. Tests are the convergence checkpoints. Without them, you produce spaghetti at unprecedented speed.

Git + GitHub give me branch-based work and human review. Lean methodology -- plan, architecture decision records, exit criteria, definition of done -- creates a retrocontrol framework. The model doesn't protect itself from its own errors. I have to.

This means you can't safely use these tools in a language you don't master. For throwaway code, maybe. For production, no. You need to be able to read and judge every line.

## The questions that keep me up

**Who captures the value?** If I'm 2-3x more productive, my employer gets 2-3x the output. I get the same salary and more fatigue. The tool costs 200 EUR/month. The equivalent human hours cost [orders of magnitude more](https://steve-yegge.medium.com/the-ai-vampire-eda6e4f07163). This is a value capture problem. And right now, the answer is: not the engineer.

**Where do juniors go?** You need senior experience to review LLM output, validate architecture, catch subtle bugs, manage plans. If there's [no place for juniors](https://podwise.ai/dashboard/episodes/6446247), how do you train the seniors of tomorrow? This isn't a hypothetical. I'm living it at my agency.

**What happens to our skills?** Basic neurology: unused synaptic connections get pruned. If engineers stop writing code because AI does it, their coding skill degrades. I need to seriously think about a work methodology that maintains human competence. I haven't solved this yet.

**What happens when the gap widens?** Between the current generation and the previous one, 6 months produced a massive leap. Open-source models lag about [6 months behind](https://shumer.dev/something-big-is-happening). If frontier models can contribute to building the next frontier model, that 6-month gap could become permanent. Or worse, it could widen. The sovereignty implications for a French public agency are... significant.

## What I've learned so far

Three months in, I'm operating at what I'd call a [supervisory level](https://www.danshapiro.com/blog/2026/01/the-five-levels-from-spicy-autocomplete-to-the-software-factory/). I review diffs. I write plans. I manage agents. I rarely type code character by character anymore. And I've shipped more in three months than I would have in a year working alone.

But I'm more tired. I'm more distracted. I catch myself cutting corners I wouldn't have cut before. I recognize addiction patterns in my own behavior.

The honest assessment: this is a superpower. And it's draining. Both things are true. Most people writing about AI-assisted development pick one side. The evangelists talk about the productivity. The skeptics talk about the limits. The reality is messier.

I'm a doctor who became an engineer. I've seen what happens when powerful tools meet human psychology without guardrails. It usually doesn't end with people calmly choosing the optimal dosage.

We need to talk about the human cost. Not to slow down adoption. But because the people in the cockpit need to know what the flight does to them.
